items.title: Inflation May Have Peaked in October: Economists Split on How Many Fed Hikes Are Effectively Needed
items.excerpt: A Federal Reserve inflation tracker is flashing a zero for November. The Cleveland Fed’s inflation nowcast, a daily model built on oil and gasoline prices, estimates that US consumer prices were unchanged in November from October. That would be the softest monthly reading since June, when the consumer price index fell 0.4%. So is US inflation finally near its peak? Gasoline explains most of the relief. The national average for regular gas has slipped below $3.60 a gallon, down from nearly $4.50 in late September, according to the American Automobile Association. The personal consumption expenditures (PCE) price index, the Fed’s preferred inflation gauge, rose 3.8% from a year earlier in October, the Bureau of Economic Analysis said Wednesday. “Recent declines in gasoline prices suggest that headline PCE inflation may have peaked,” HSBC economist Ryan Wang said in a note Wednesday. Wang expects one final quarter-point hike in December, lifting the federal funds target range to 4.00%-4.25%, and then no change through 2027. ... The same Cleveland Fed nowcast puts November headline PCE at 3.78%, slightly below October’s 3.84%. Meanwhile, it sees core PCE rising further to 3.38%. Pantheon Macroeconomics chief US economist Samuel Tombs expects core PCE to peak at 3.4% in November before easing to 3.0% by May 2027. Still, he does not see energy as the only culprit. “The breadth of momentum in services prices points to some demand-driven inflation too,” Tombs said.

items.title: GDP (Second Estimate) and Corporate Profits, 3rd Quarter 2026 | U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA)
items.excerpt: EMBARGOED UNTIL RELEASE AT 8:30 a.m. EST, Wednesday, November 25, 2026 # GDP (Second Estimate) and Corporate Profits, 3rd Quarter 2026 Real gross domestic product (GDP) increased at an annual rate of 4.3 percent in the third quarter of 2026 (July, August, and September), according to the second estimate released today by the U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA). In the second quarter, real GDP increased 2.2 percent. The contributors to the increase in real GDP in the third quarter were increases in investment, consumer spending, and government spending that were partly offset by a decrease in exports. Imports, which are a subtraction in the calculation of GDP, increased. Real GDP was revised up 0.9 percentage point from the advance estimate, primarily reflecting upward revisions to investment and consumer spending. For more information, refer to the " Technical Notes" below. Compared to the second quarter, the acceleration in real GDP in the third quarter primarily reflected an acceleration in investment and an upturn in government spending that were partly offset by a downturn in exports. Imports increased more in the third quarter than in the second quarter. Real final sales to private domestic purchasers, the sum of consumer spending and gross private fixed investment, increased 5.8 percent in the third quarter, revised up 0.9 percentage point from the previous estimate. The price index for gross domestic purchases increased 2.7 percent in the third quarter, revised down 0.3 percentage point from the previous estimate. The personal consumption expenditures (PCE) price index increased 2.1 percent, and the PCE price index, excluding food and energy increased 2.5 percent, both the same as previously estimated. Real gross domestic income (GDI) increased 4.4 percent in the third quarter, compared with an increase of 2.3 percent (revised) in the second quarter. The average of real GDP and real GDI also increased 4.4 percent, compared with an increase of 2.2 percent (revised). Profits from current production (corporate profits with inventory valuation and capital consumption adjustments) increased $206.0 billion in the third quarter, compared with an increase of $384.0 billion in the second quarter.

items.title: Trump administration proposes new tariffs on goods from major U.S. trading partners : NPR
items.excerpt: November 26, 2026 6:43 AM ET Heard on Morning Edition ... President Trump's new proposed tariffs are already meeting pushback from Democrats and some free trade advocates. Transcript A MARTÍNEZ, HOST: The Trump administration is proposing new tariffs on goods from 14 of the U.S.'s biggest trading partners, including Japan, the EU and China. It's arguing that these new tariffs fight other countries' unfair trade practices, but it's not clear that they will actually do that. For more, we have NPR White House correspondent Danielle Kurtzleben. Danielle, what did the White House outline yesterday? DANIELLE KURTZLEBEN, BYLINE: Well, it's new proposed tariffs on goods from major trading partners - the ones you mentioned, and also South Korea and Cambodia, for example. And the rates could go as high as 40% on Chinese goods, also 35% on goods from Vietnam and 20 or 25% on goods from other countries. They're also proposing additional tariffs on sugar and aircrafts from Brazil, and that would add to previous tariffs the U.S. imposed there. MARTÍNEZ: When could these plans actually become real? KURTZLEBEN: Well, they could go into effect within a couple of months. That's what U.S. Trade Ambassador Jamieson Greer said yesterday. Now, as for what the rates will be, well, that's still unclear, and that's because for each country, excepting those additional tariffs on Brazil, the White House has two rates they've listed - a proposed rate and a deal rate. To give an example, the tariff on China could be 20%. That's the deal rate. But depending in part on how ongoing discussions go, the rates on Chinese goods could go as high as 40%. MARTÍNEZ: Forty percent. Now, yeah, the Supreme Court struck down some of Trump's earlier tariffs. So how is the White House legally justifying these new ones? KURTZLEBEN: Well, these are being implemented under a law known for short as Section 301, which is meant to counter other countries' unfair trade practices. And so here the White House is alleging that these other countries have what's called structural excess capacity in various manufactured goods. And the administration has described this as when another country has policies that cause a good to be overproduced, which then distorts a global market for that good. And so those practices, according to the administration, can include all sorts of things, like labor practices, subsidies and tax breaks. Now, the administration imposed other sweeping 301 tariffs earlier this year, and there's a lawsuit in process challenging those, with the key argument being that those tariffs were just way broader than the 301 law calls for. MARTÍNEZ: Now, you mentioned a lawsuit. Could these new tariffs face similar legal challenges? KURTZLEBEN: You know, they could. We'll see what happens. But I talked to Sara Albrecht. She's chairman and CEO of the nonpartisan Liberty and Justice Center (ph), which filed that lawsuit against those earlier tariffs. And she said these new tariffs are not being used the way 301 tariffs are supposed to. SARA ALBRECHT: It is a negotiating tactic. That is not what tariffs, in a broad sense, are supposed to be. Like, you can do that on a country-by-country basis if they're addressing a specific problem, not just general, hey, we want better trade deals. KURTZLEBEN: In addition, both she and other trade experts say they think the White House is just proposing these new tariffs as a way to replace the sweeping tariffs the Supreme Court struck down earlier this year. MARTÍNEZ: Now, we all just found out how unpopular these tariffs were in the midterm elections. So how are these new tariffs landing politically? KURTZLEBEN: Well, we've heard some real pushback from congressional Democrats. Richard Neal, top House Democrat on the Ways and Means Committee, said in a statement, quote, "Trump is putting everything from family budgets to our national security at risk to keep his tariff scheme in place." Now, congressional Republicans have been quieter, and this does come a few weeks after they lost dozens of seats in the election, which is widely attributed, in large part, to high prices, and tariffs do cause higher prices.

items.excerpt: Second Judge Blocks Trump Birthright Citizenship Order A second federal judge on Wednesday blocked the Trump administration’s latest effort to restrict birthright citizenship. U.S. District Judge Christopher R. Cooper of Washington, D.C., issued a preliminary injunction in a 67-page opinion, The Hill reported. The order prevents federal authorities from enforcing the president’s August executive orders, which sought to narrow who qualifies for citizenship at birth. Cooper wrote that the Supreme Court “has twice confirmed that all children born in this country are U.S. citizens, save only for the small handful who are not subject to U.S. law.” A federal judge in Maryland blocked the administration’s effort in September. 3 Judge Halts FCC Early Review of ABC Station Licenses A federal ... Defense lawyer Delphine Meillet told the Associated Press in a written message Thursday that the 77-year-old actor would face trial over only one of two alleged rapes reported by actress Charlotte Arnould. Depardieu has denied the allegations. The development comes less than two weeks after Depardieu abandoned his appeal against a sexual assault conviction in a separate case. He was convicted in May 2025 of groping two women on a film set in 2021. The cases have put one of French cinema’s most celebrated figures at the center of the country’s #MeToo reckoning. Angelina Jolie and Brad Pitt settle winery fight lawsuit that surfaced abuse allegations LOS ANGELES (AP) — Angelina Jolie and Brad Pitt have settled their long-running legal battles over a French winery. In a joint statement Wednesday, they announced the settlement, saying it's in the best interests of their family. Jolie filed for divorce in 2016, alleging Pitt abused her and their children during a flight. The FBI investigated but didn't pursue charges. The winery lawsuit revealed more details of the abuse allegations and their split, with Pitt accusing Jolie of selling her share without his consent. Both actors have remained private about their breakup, focusing on their careers and family. Gordon Ramsay to take the lead in revival of BBC's flagship motoring program 'Top Gear' LONDON (AP) — Gordon Ramsay, the renowned British chef and restaurateur who has forged a successful career on television, will lead the revival of the BBC’s motoring program “Top Gear.” Ramsay, whose hit shows on both sides of the Atlantic include “Hell’s Kitchen” and “Ramsay’s Kitchen Nightmares,” said Wednesday that he “can’t wait to get started.” Filming will take place across the U.K., including at the show’s Dunsfold Aerodrome base southwest of London and around the world next year, for broadcast in 2028. “Top Gear” has been off air since 2022 when former cricketer Andrew Flintoff was seriously injured, during filming.
